suggestion_note: PARITY CORRECTION. v1 English said 'a drooping face'; French 'le visage deforme' and Swahili 'uso umepinda' say face too. The Kinyarwanda says MOUTH — 'umunwa wagoramye' in v1 and 'umunwa we waragoramye' in the speaker's third. A twisted mouth is what a family sees; a drooping face is the stroke exam. NOTE: the Kinyarwanda FIRST person is unauthored, so this row has no speaker text to check against — only their third.

suggested_english: {REL} cannot speak properly and their mouth has gone crooked
suggestion_note: person transform. USES SINGULAR 'THEIR' AND NEEDS A RULING. This is the non-obstetric counterpart of the obstetric 'she': ALL_RELATIONS spans both genders, so a possessive forces a choice English cannot avoid and Kinyarwanda never faces ('umunwa we' is neutral). Singular 'their' is the neutral option and reads acceptably after 'My child'; it reads slightly oddly after 'My father'. The alternatives are to drop the possessive, which is not natural English here, or to expand the phrase into two per gender, which doubles a phrase for no clinical gain. Provisional — one ruling settles every non-obstetric third with a possessive.
